items.title: Unit 4: Ask Questions, Look for Evidence, STEM Unit Project (What's inside the Moon?)

question.html: For a unit on how waves reveal hidden structure, a class wants to know what is inside the Moon. Write three good investigation questions, say what evidence would help, and outline a first step for a project.

body.html: This is an open-ended, class-style prompt (questions on sticky notes, a Summary Table, a unit project start).

Seismometers left on the Moon recorded "moonquakes." Like earthquake waves, moonquake waves speed up, slow down, bend (refract) and partly bounce (reflect) where the material changes. Transverse (S-type) waves cannot pass through a liquid, so a shadow zone for S waves suggests a liquid or partly molten layer.

answer.html: Questions: "How do moonquake waves change speed with depth?", "Do any wave types fail to reach the far side of the Moon?", "How does the arrival-time pattern tell us where layer boundaries are?" Evidence to collect: arrival times of waves at several stations, and which wave types arrive at each. Project start: draw a cross-section, place a quake and several stations, and sketch the ray paths that bend at each boundary. Your own board, Summary Table and project must be done with your class; this is a model starting point.

check.html: No single numerical answer exists, so this is a representative response.

items.title: Module 13 Encounter the Phenomenon, Ask Questions, and Make Your Claim (CER)

question.html: How can a long footbridge that starts swaying when many people walk across it be calmed down?

body.html: A bridge has natural frequencies. Walkers push sideways at about the walking-step frequency, so if that matches a natural frequency of the bridge the sway builds up (resonance). Engineers add dampers that remove vibrational energy, or change the bridge's natural frequency by stiffening or adding mass.

answer.html: Adding dampers that absorb the bridge's vibrational energy, or shifting the bridge's natural frequency away from the walking frequency, stops resonance from growing the sway. Sample extra questions: "How do engineers measure the bridge's natural frequency?", "How much energy must the dampers remove each cycle?"

check.html: The claim uses the idea (from this module) that a driving force at the natural frequency gives the biggest amplitude.

items.title: Focus Question: What are some examples of motion that repeats?

answer.html: A swinging door that rocks back and forth, a mass hanging from a spring that bobs up and down, a plucked guitar string, a swing set, and a metronome arm are all periodic. When the restoring force is proportional to the displacement (an ideal spring, or a pendulum at small angles) the motion is simple harmonic motion.

items.title: 8: Why is a mass bobbing on a vertical spring an example of periodic motion?

answer.html: The mass repeats the same up-and-down path in a fixed time (its period). The net force (spring force plus weight) always points toward the equilibrium position, so the mass is pulled back every time it moves away, and each cycle repeats the last.

items.title: 12: A bicycle rattles badly at one particular speed on a washboard road with evenly spaced bumps, but not at slower or faster speeds. Explain.

answer.html: Evenly spaced bumps push on the bike at a frequency equal to the speed divided by the bump spacing. At the one speed where this driving frequency equals a natural frequency of the bike's frame and wheels, each push adds to the motion in step with it: resonance, which builds large amplitude. At other speeds the pushes do not match the natural frequency, so the shaking stays small.

items.title: 13 (Critical Thinking): How are a ball moving at constant speed around a circle and a mass bobbing on a spring similar and different?

answer.html: Similar: both are periodic and repeat after one period, and in both the net force points toward the center or equilibrium position. The shadow of the ball on a wall moves up and down exactly like the mass on a spring (simple harmonic motion). Different: circular motion is two- dimensional at constant speed with a force of constant size, while the spring motion is one- dimensional, its speed changes (zero at the ends, maximum at the center), and the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, ranging from zero to maximum.

items.title: Unit 4: Ask Questions, Look for Evidence, STEM Unit Project (What's inside Earth?)

body.html: These are open-ended, class-based prompts (write questions on sticky notes, keep a Summary Table, start a unit project).

Earthquake waves (P waves are longitudinal, S waves are transverse) change speed and direction (refract and reflect) at boundaries inside Earth. Because S waves cannot travel through liquids, and wave speeds jump at certain depths, scientists infer layers such as a liquid outer core.

answer.html: Sample questions for the board: "How do waves carry energy without moving matter?", "Why do waves bend or bounce at boundaries?", "How can wave speeds tell us what a material is made of?" For the project, the key evidence is that wave speed and direction change at boundaries, so waves recorded far from an earthquake reveal the layers they passed through. Your own board, Summary Table, and project report must be done in class; this is a model starting point.

check.html: The prompts have no single numerical answer, so this is a representative response.

items.title: Module 13 Encounter the Phenomenon, Ask Questions, and Make Your Claim (CER)

question.html: How can a pendulum save a building from earthquake damage?

body.html: A building is a vibrating system with its own natural frequency. Earthquake shaking can drive it at resonance, so the swaying grows (Lesson 1). A massive pendulum (a tuned mass damper) hung in the building has a period 𝑇= 2𝜋√ℓ/ 𝑔 chosen to match the building's sway period. When the building sways, the pendulum swings out of step with the building, so it pushes back against the motion and absorbs energy, which the dampers turn into thermal energy.

answer.html: A heavy pendulum tuned to the building's natural period absorbs the building's vibrational energy, shrinking the sway amplitude and preventing resonance damage. Sample extra questions: "How do engineers pick the pendulum's length and mass?", "What does the hydraulic damper do?"

check.html: Consistent with the book's pendulum result that the period depends on length and g, not on the mass or amplitude.

answer.html: A mass bobbing on a spring, a swinging pendulum, a vibrating guitar string, and a child's swing being pushed are all periodic motion. When the restoring force is proportional to the displacement (spring with Hooke's law, pendulum at small angles), the motion is simple harmonic motion.

items.title: Physics Challenge (car and crash barrier): (a) maximum compression, (b) effect of doubling the height, (c) what happens afterward

body.html: Car mass 𝑚, starts at rest at height ℎ, frictionless, hits a spring of constant 𝑘 at the bottom. Find the maximum compression 𝑥.

Conservation of energy: gravitational PE at the top becomes spring PE at maximum compression (the car is momentarily at rest). We treat the small extra drop during compression as negligible compared with ℎ. Work (a):

answer.html: 𝑥= √2𝑚𝑔ℎ/ 𝑘 Work (b): Replace ℎ with 2ℎ: 𝑥′ = √2𝑚𝑔(2ℎ) / 𝑘= √2 𝑥.

The compression increases by a factor of √2 ≈1.41. Work (c): At maximum compression the spring still pushes on the car with force 𝑘𝑥. With no friction, the stored energy is returned: the spring pushes the car back out and back up the hill, and in the ideal case it would return to height ℎ and repeat forever.

The car is pushed back up the hill (the spring releases its energy), oscillating until friction or a latch/damper removes the energy. A real barrier is designed to dissipate that energy so the car does not rebound.

check.html: 𝑥 has units √kg · m/s<sup>2</sup> · m / (N/m) = m.

answer.html: A pendulum repeats the same back-and-forth path in a fixed time (its period). The restoring force (a component of gravity) always points toward the equilibrium position, so each swing repeats the last one.

answer.html: If the data fall on a straight line through the origin (force proportional to stretch), the rubber band obeys Hooke's law, and the slope is 𝑘. If the graph is curved, or the slope changes, it does not obey Hooke's law. (Rubber bands generally are curved.)

answer.html: To double the period, make the pendulum 4 times as long. To halve it, make the length one- fourth as long.

items.title: 12: A car shakes strongly at one specific speed (unbalanced wheel). Explain.

answer.html: An unbalanced wheel pushes on the car once per wheel rotation, so the wheel's rotation rate sets the frequency of a periodic force. At the particular speed where this frequency equals a natural frequency of the car's suspension and body, the force pushes in step with the motion: resonance, which builds large amplitude. At higher or lower speeds the driving frequency does not match, so the shaking is small.

items.title: 13 (Critical Thinking): How are uniform circular motion and simple harmonic motion similar and different?

answer.html: Similar: both are periodic, repeating after one period, and both have a force directed toward the center or equilibrium position. In fact, the shadow of an object in uniform circular motion moves in simple harmonic motion. Different: circular motion is two-dimensional at constant speed with a constant-magnitude force; SHM is one-dimensional, its speed changes (zero at the ends, maximum at the center), and the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, changing from zero to maximum.
